lessons.title: How to Edit Videos (COMPLETE Beginner's Guide)
objectives: Name the stages every edit goes through, in order
Cut for the story rather than trimming clips at random
Set up a project so you can still find your footage next week
lessons.notes:
Every edit, on every piece of software, follows the same order. Learn the order and the software becomes a detail.

1. IMPORT AND ORGANISE. Get the footage in and named. This is the boring step everyone skips, and it is why beginners lose an afternoon looking for a clip.

2. ASSEMBLE. Lay the shots out in rough order. Do not tidy anything yet. You are finding the shape.

3. CUT. Remove everything that does not earn its place. This is the actual craft, and almost all of it is subtraction.

4. AUDIO. Levels, background noise, music. More on this in Module 3, and it matters more than anyone expects.

5. COLOUR. Make the shots match each other, then set a look.

6. TITLES AND GRAPHICS. Last, so you are not re-doing them after a cut.

7. EXPORT. Out to a file someone can actually watch.

The single rule under all of it: CUT FOR THE STORY. Before every cut, ask what the viewer needs next. Not what looks clever — what they need. The most common beginner fault is a video that shows everything that was filmed, in the order it was filmed.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — how you set up matters more here than in most places. Make one folder per project with subfolders for footage, audio, and exports, and keep a second copy of the raw footage somewhere else. Video files are large and corrupt easily, phones fill up, and re-shooting a client's event is not an option. Also: your editing software does not contain your footage. It contains directions to it. Move or rename the files and the project opens empty, which is the most alarming thing that will happen to you this month and is entirely recoverable if you know it is coming.
lessons.practice: Take any footage you already have — even phone clips from an event — and cut it to exactly 60 seconds following the seven stages in order. Organise and rename first, before you cut anything. Then the hard part: cut another 20 seconds out of your finished 60. What you leave in when forced to choose is what the video was actually about.

quiz.question: What is the main skill in the cutting stage?
options: Subtraction — removing everything that does not earn its place
Adding transitions between every shot
Keeping the footage in the order it was filmed
Making each clip the same length

quiz.question: Why does your project open empty after you move your footage?
options: The project file stores directions to the footage, not the footage itself
The software deleted the clips
The files became corrupted
The project expired

lessons.title: Best Video Editing App in 2026
objectives: Choose an editor by what your machine and your work actually need
Understand what separates a free editor from a paid one
Avoid paying a subscription before you have been paid
lessons.notes:
The honest answer to 'which editor is best' is: the one that runs on the machine you own. Everything else is a preference.

The categories, with the part reviews leave out:

PHONE EDITORS — CapCut and its equivalents. Genuinely capable, free at entry level, and the right starting point if you do not own a capable laptop. A large share of paid social video work is edited entirely on a phone, and clients do not ask.

FREE DESKTOP EDITORS — DaVinci Resolve is the significant one: a professional tool, free, used on actual films. It is demanding on hardware and steep to learn. If your laptop struggles with it, that is the laptop, not you.

SUBSCRIPTION EDITORS — the industry-standard desktop tools. Real advantages in collaboration and integration, and a monthly cost in foreign currency that is a serious commitment here. Do not start one until a client is paying for it.

WHAT ACTUALLY MATTERS on a modest machine, in order: enough RAM, storage that is not full, and the ability to edit PROXIES — small stand-in copies of your footage that keep the timeline responsive, with the full-quality files swapped back in for export. Proxy editing is the single technique that makes heavy footage workable on light hardware, and it is why 'my laptop is too slow to edit' is often solvable.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — skills transfer between these tools far more than tutorials imply. Timeline, cut, transition, keyframe, export all exist in every one of them under slightly different names. Learn one properly and you can move. Do not wait for better software before you start; start on what you have and let a paying client fund the upgrade.
lessons.practice: Edit the same 30-second clip twice — once on a phone editor, once on a free desktop editor. Time both, including the export. Note which one frustrated you and where. Then check whether your desktop editor supports proxies and turn them on. That answer decides what you should be working on for the next month.

quiz.question: What makes heavy footage editable on a modest laptop?
options: Editing proxies — small stand-in copies, with full-quality files restored for export
Buying a subscription editor
Shortening every clip before importing
Exporting at a lower resolution

quiz.question: When should you start paying for a subscription editor?
options: When a paying client makes it necessary, not before
As soon as you begin learning
Once you have watched enough tutorials
Never — paid editors have no advantages

lessons.title: How to Use CapCut Video Editing
objectives: Complete a full edit on a phone, from import to export
Use the timeline tools that do most of the work
Export at settings that suit where the video is going
lessons.notes:
This is where you stop watching and start editing. CapCut is free, runs on a phone, and does more than a beginner needs.

The tools that do ninety per cent of the work: SPLIT (cut a clip in two), DELETE, SPEED, VOLUME, and TEXT. Learn those five properly before you touch anything else. Beginners collect effects and never learn to cut; effects do not fix a badly cut video and cannot hide one.

A working order on a phone: import, cut the video down to what it is about, get the audio right, add text, add music, export. Same seven stages from Module 1, smaller screen.

EXPORT SETTINGS, which tutorials rush and which matter most here:
- RESOLUTION. 1080p is right for almost everything. 4K produces enormous files, and if the footage was not shot in 4K it adds nothing at all.
- FRAME RATE. Match what you filmed at. Changing it introduces stutter.
- SHAPE. Vertical (9:16) for TikTok, Reels and Status. Horizontal (16:9) for YouTube and television. Decide BEFORE you edit — reframing an entire video afterwards is miserable and it always shows.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — the practical Kenyan details. Watch the WATERMARK: free tiers add one, and delivering watermarked work to a client is unprofessional; find the setting and check the exported file, not the preview. Watch the FILE SIZE: a client receiving a 2GB file on a bundle will not thank you, so export sensibly and send a link rather than the file itself where you can. And expect to deliver on WhatsApp, which compresses heavily — send the real file through a link or as a document so the client sees the quality they paid for.
lessons.practice: Edit a complete 60-second video on your phone using only split, delete, speed, volume and text. Export it twice: once vertical for social, once horizontal. Compare the file sizes, then send one to yourself over WhatsApp both as a normal video and as a document, and look at the difference in quality. That difference is what your client sees.

quiz.question: When should you decide whether a video is vertical or horizontal?
options: Before editing — reframing afterwards is painful and visible
After exporting
During colour grading
It does not matter

quiz.question: Why send a client a link rather than the video file on WhatsApp?
options: WhatsApp compresses video heavily, so the client sees worse quality than you delivered
Links are more professional
Video files cannot be sent on WhatsApp
It is faster to upload

lessons.title: How to Create Video Transitions
objectives: Use a cut as the default and a transition as the exception
Match a transition to what is happening in the story
Recognise the effects that mark an edit as amateur
lessons.notes:
The most important thing about transitions is how rarely professionals use them.

Watch anything well made and count. Almost every change of shot is a straight CUT. No spin, no zoom, no swoosh. The cut is invisible, and invisible is the goal — the viewer should be following the story, not noticing your editing.

When a transition is genuinely right:
- A CROSS DISSOLVE for a passage of time, or a gentle change of mood.
- A FADE TO BLACK to end a section or the video.
- A MATCH CUT, where something in one shot lines up with something in the next. This is the one worth practising; it is the transition that looks expensive and costs nothing.

What marks a beginner instantly: a different flashy transition between every shot, effects applied because they were in the library, and transitions used to hide the fact that two shots do not belong together. That last one never works — if the join feels wrong, the problem is the shots or the order, and a spin will not fix it.

The test before adding any transition: WHAT IS THIS TELLING THE VIEWER? 'Time passed', 'we are somewhere new', 'this section is over' are answers. 'It looked cool' is not.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — there is a genuine exception, and you should know it because it may be what you are paid for. Fast, obvious transitions are a deliberate style in short-form social video, where they hold attention in the first seconds. That is a real choice for a real context, not an accident. The rule is not 'never use transitions' — it is 'know which you are doing and why', and be able to say so when a client asks.
lessons.practice: Take a sequence you have already cut with transitions and remove every one, leaving straight cuts. Watch it back. Most will be better. Then add back only the ones that answer 'what is this telling the viewer', and write the answer down for each. If you cannot write it, take it out again.

quiz.question: What should the default change of shot be?
options: A straight cut — invisible, so the viewer follows the story
A cross dissolve
A fade to black
A different effect each time, for variety

quiz.question: Two shots feel wrong next to each other. What is the fix?
options: Change the shots or their order — a transition will not fix a bad join
A longer dissolve
A flashy transition to distract from it
A fade to black between them

lessons.title: How to Color Grade in DaVinci Resolve for Beginners
objectives: Separate correcting a shot from styling it
Make shots from different moments match each other
Judge colour on something other than your own screen
lessons.notes:
Colour work is two jobs, and doing them in the wrong order is why beginners' grades look strange.

CORRECTION comes first. Make the shot look right: exposure so it is neither crushed dark nor blown white, white balance so white things are white, contrast so it is not flat. Correction is objective — there is a right answer, and your eyes are not it.

GRADING comes second. Now choose a look: warmer, cooler, richer, muted. This is taste, and it should be consistent across the whole video.

Between them sits the job that actually earns money: MATCHING. Footage shot at different times of day, or on two different phones, will not match. Getting a sequence to feel like one continuous piece is the difference between a video that looks professional and one that looks assembled, and it is mostly correction rather than style.

USE THE SCOPES, not your eyes. Every serious editor shows you a waveform or a histogram — a graph of the actual brightness and colour in the frame. Your eyes adapt within seconds and lie to you; the scope does not. Learning to read one thing, the waveform, puts you ahead of most people editing on phones.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — the constraint that matters in practice: YOU CANNOT TRUST YOUR SCREEN. A cheap laptop panel, a phone in bright sun, an uncalibrated monitor — each shows different colour. Before delivering, check the export on at least two other devices, ideally including a phone, since that is where it will be watched. And go lighter than feels right: a grade that looks pleasantly moody on your screen often looks muddy on a phone outdoors, which is where your Kenyan audience is actually watching.
lessons.practice: Take three clips shot at different times or on different devices and make them match — correction only, no look. Use the waveform rather than your eyes. Then apply one consistent grade across all three, export, and view it on a phone outdoors in daylight. Adjust based on what you see there, not on what you saw on your laptop.

quiz.question: What is the correct order of colour work?
options: Correct the shot first, then match shots to each other, then apply a look
Apply the look first, then correct
Match first, then correct, then style
Any order gives the same result

quiz.question: Why check the exported video on a phone outdoors?
options: A grade that looks moody on a laptop often looks muddy where the audience actually watches
Phones display more colours
It compresses the file
Daylight improves colour accuracy

lessons.title: 5 Basic Audio-Mixing Techniques for Editing Video
objectives: Set dialogue and music to levels that work on a phone speaker
Reduce background noise without making a voice sound artificial
Treat audio as the half of the video most likely to lose a viewer
lessons.notes:
Viewers forgive bad pictures. They will not sit through bad sound, and they leave without knowing why. If you have an hour left before delivery, spend it on audio.

The five things that do the work:

LEVELS. Dialogue should sit consistently, without jumping between speakers or shots. The commonest fault is a video where one section is fine and the next needs the volume turned up.

MUSIC UNDER VOICE. Music should sit clearly below dialogue — noticeably quieter, not slightly. When both compete, the viewer strains, and straining is how you lose them.

NOISE REDUCTION. Fans, traffic, matatu hooting, room hum. Reduce it gently. Pushed too hard, noise reduction makes a voice sound thin and underwater, which is worse than the noise.

FADES. Never let music or sound start or stop abruptly. A short fade in and out on every audio clip is a two-second habit that removes a whole category of amateur-sounding edit.

ROOM TONE. The quiet sound of the space itself. Keep a few seconds of it and use it to fill silences, so that cuts do not drop into complete digital silence, which the ear hears as a mistake.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — mix for the speaker your audience has, which is a phone, often in a noisy place. Check your mix at low volume on a phone speaker, not on headphones. What is comfortable on headphones frequently has inaudible dialogue on a phone. And where you can influence the shoot: getting the microphone close to the speaker's mouth beats any amount of repair afterwards. Bad audio can be improved. It cannot be fixed.
lessons.practice: Take a video you have edited and work only on its audio: even out the dialogue, drop the music clearly under the voice, apply gentle noise reduction, fade every audio clip in and out, and fill any silence with room tone. Then listen on a phone speaker at low volume, somewhere noisy. Fix what you cannot hear there, not what you cannot hear on headphones.

quiz.question: Where should you check your final mix?
options: On a phone speaker at low volume, in a noisy place — where the audience actually listens
On good headphones only
On a laptop at full volume
In the editing software preview

quiz.question: What happens when noise reduction is pushed too far?
options: The voice becomes thin and artificial, which is worse than the original noise
The file size increases
The video goes out of sync
The music becomes louder
